strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the paper is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks plus Applied/Systems analysis rather than a new-algorithm paper; under that lens, the central contribution is valuable: a scaled two-dot behavioral benchmark on natural COCO scenes with 72 participants, eye-tracking control, counterbalancing, and 1020 object-grouping trials.

The paper asks an interesting and timely question for computer vision: whether self-supervised vision foundation models encode object structure in a way aligned with human perceptual grouping, rather than only with downstream segmentation or recognition metrics.

The experimental story is coherent across multiple measurements: DINO-family models perform best on same/different grouping accuracy, predict human reaction times better, show higher object-centric ROC/AUC from patch affinities, and improve supervised models when their Gram structure is distilled from DINOv3.

The comparison includes several meaningful axes: transformer vs convolutional architectures, supervised vs self-supervised objectives, ImageNet-1K vs larger-data pretraining, MAE vs DINO-style self-distillation, and a distilled ConvNeXt model. This makes the main qualitative conclusion about the importance of training objective more persuasive.

The object-centric affinity/ROC analysis is intuitive, visually interpretable, and connects model representations to both object masks and behavioral alignment. The correlation between object-centric AUC and noise-normalized RT prediction is a useful mechanistic bridge.
The manuscript is generally clear and well motivated, with good links to classical perceptual grouping, association fields, and recent evidence on emergent object-centricity in self-supervised ViTs.
weaknesses: The strongest methodological concern is the reaction-time prediction protocol: 10-fold cross-validation is described at the trial level over 1020 behavioral trials, but each image contributes four related dot conditions. If folds are not split by image, the readout may train on the same image in other conditions and test on a held-out dot placement, inflating behavioral-alignment estimates. A leave-image-out split, and ideally leave-category/object-pair-out analysis, is needed.

The paper relies heavily on learned MLP readouts, which makes it harder to isolate representation quality from readout capacity and dataset-specific supervision. Simpler baselines such as dot distance, same/different COCO mask labels, low-level color/texture similarity, CLIP features, linear readouts, and ground-truth object-mask predictors would clarify how much of the RT variance is genuinely model-representational rather than task- or dataset-driven.

Statistical reporting is thin. Figures show rankings and improvements but provide few confidence intervals, standard errors across images/subjects/seeds, significance tests, or uncertainty for the correlations between object-centricity and behavior. With only nine model points in the cross-model correlation, claims about a general principle should be stated more cautiously.

The benchmark construction depends on COCO object annotations and manual filtering, but the paper does not fully characterize possible selection bias. Images are selected to have a central object and overlapping second object with valid placements, which may favor certain object sizes, categories, textures, and occlusion structures. Category-level and image-property analyses would help establish generality.

The object-centric AUC metric is evaluated against COCO object masks rather than directly against human segmentation judgments. This is reasonable for a proxy metric, but it weakens claims that the metric measures human object perception itself, especially in ambiguous scenes where humans may group parts, occluders, or contextual objects differently from COCO annotations.

The Gram-alignment experiment is promising but under-specified. The manuscript does not give enough details about the exact loss, weighting against ImageNet classification, training data, schedule, compute, checkpoint selection, or whether ImageNet accuracy is actually preserved. Without this, the causal interpretation that Gram structure actively drives alignment is suggestive rather than fully demonstrated.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence supports. For example, saying training objective matters more than architecture is plausible within the tested set, but architecture, pretraining data, distillation target, model generation, and dense-feature training recipe are partially confounded. DINOv3 ConvNeXt is distilled from a DINOv3 teacher, so it is not an independent architecture-only comparison.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone: there is no clear code/data release statement, no full list of model checkpoints and preprocessing details, no MLP hyperparameters, no training details for the 30k generated trials, and no subject/image split files. These details matter because the claims rest on relatively specialized behavioral stimuli and readout procedures.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and relevant question: whether modern self-supervised vision models, especially DINO-family ViTs, capture object grouping structure in a way that aligns with human perceptual behavior in natural scenes.

The behavioral two-dot paradigm is well motivated by prior psychophysics, and scaling it to natural COCO scenes with eye tracking and counterbalanced same/different, close/far conditions is a useful empirical direction.

The comparison across self-supervised, supervised, transformer, and convolutional models is conceptually valuable, and the broad finding that DINO-style objectives yield more object-centric patch similarity is plausible and potentially interesting.

The paper attempts to connect behavioral alignment, patch-level object-centricity, and Gram-matrix structure, which could be a meaningful bridge between psychophysics and representation analysis if supported more rigorously.
weaknesses: The main experimental evidence is not yet convincing enough for the strength of the claims. The reaction-time prediction uses 10-fold cross-validation over 1,020 trials, but because each image appears in four conditions, random trial-level splits likely leak image-specific information between train and test. A grouped split by image is essential for evaluating generalization.

The behavioral alignment model is a flexible 2-layer MLP trained directly on the same small behavioral benchmark it is evaluated on. Without stronger controls, simpler baselines, and image-held-out validation, it is hard to know whether the reported correlations reflect human-like grouping or task/dataset-specific fitting.

The object-centricity metric is presented as novel and not requiring object-level supervision, but its evaluation explicitly depends on COCO object masks/boundaries. The metric is close to a standard affinity-versus-mask segmentation evaluation, and the paper does not clearly distinguish what is new relative to existing dense descriptor, TokenCut/LOST, and self-supervised segmentation analyses.

Important quantitative details are missing or underreported: Fig. 4, Fig. 6, and Fig. 7 do not provide exact values, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or uncertainty over subjects/images/seeds. Claims such as “strongly correlated” and “consistently improves” need statistical support.

The Gram alignment section is especially under-specified. The paper does not give the loss formulation, weighting relative to classification, optimization details, data regime, compute, or whether ImageNet validation accuracy is preserved. This makes the result hard to reproduce and hard to interpret.

The Gram alignment evidence is partly circular: supervised models are trained to match DINOv3 Gram structure and then evaluated using metrics that reward DINO-like patch similarity/object-centricity. Stronger independent tests are needed to show that this intervention causally improves human-like perception rather than simply moving models toward the teacher representation.

The model comparison is incomplete for the stated conclusions. Missing baselines include CLIP/SigLIP-style models, SAM or segmentation-pretrained models, simple low-level feature/distance/color/edge baselines, and explicit COCO-mask or object-size/category controls. These are needed to establish that the reported alignment is not driven by easier confounds.

The grouping accuracy experiment is not clearly tied to human behavior: the classifier is trained on COCO-derived same/different labels and evaluated on COCO-derived labels, while human accuracy is around 90%. DINOv3 reaching 91.9% on this label task does not by itself demonstrate human-like perception.

The paper often overstates mechanistic conclusions. For example, it claims Gram matrix structure is an “active contributor” and a “fundamental organizing principle” of human-like visual representations, but the evidence is correlational plus teacher distillation, not a clean causal or mechanistic account.

Reproducibility is limited: the manuscript does not clearly commit to releasing the behavioral dataset, dot placements, preprocessing code, model checkpoints after Gram alignment, or exact training/evaluation protocols. Given the custom dataset and many implementation-sensitive choices, this is a substantial concern.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and meaningful question: whether self-supervised vision representations align with human object grouping in natural scenes. The contribution is well suited to an Algorithms/General evaluation, with a strong behavioral/model-analysis component rather than a conventional new architecture paper.

The behavioral benchmark is a clear strength. The two-dot paradigm is grounded in prior psychophysics, scaled to 1020 natural-image trials with 72 participants, eye tracking, counterbalancing, matched dot distances, and sensible filtering for ambiguous annotations.

The empirical story is coherent across several measures: DINO-family self-supervised ViTs perform best on grouping accuracy, behavioral RT prediction, and the proposed object-centric ROC/AUC measure; DINOv3 ConvNeXt helps disentangle training signal from architecture; and the Gram-alignment experiments provide an interesting intervention rather than only correlational probing.

The object-centricity metric is simple, interpretable, and useful: measuring whether patch affinities remain within annotated object boundaries gives a direct bridge between dense visual representations and human grouping behavior.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with figures that communicate the main qualitative effects. The work connects CV representation learning, dense features, and human perceptual organization in a way likely to be useful beyond this specific benchmark.
weaknesses: Some methodological details needed for reproducibility are under-specified, especially the MLP architecture/training protocol, feature preprocessing, cross-validation split construction, Gram-alignment loss weighting, fine-tuning schedule, and whether code/data will be released.

The RT prediction evaluation may be optimistic if random 10-fold splits allow different conditions from the same image to appear in both train and test. A stricter image-held-out split would better test generalization to unseen scenes and reduce image-specific leakage.

The Gram-alignment result is intriguing but the causal claim is somewhat stronger than the evidence. Fine-tuning with a DINOv3 teacher changes more than Gram structure alone unless ablations are provided, such as alternative teachers, shuffled or local Gram targets, loss-weight sweeps, and controls showing ImageNet performance is preserved.

The model comparison is useful but incomplete for a broad ECCV claim about vision foundation models. Important baselines such as CLIP/SigLIP-style contrastive models, SAM/SAM2 or segmentation-oriented encoders, modern supervised foundation backbones, and larger/smaller model-scale controls would make the conclusions more robust.

The behavioral benchmark is carefully collected, but its scope is still constrained: COCO images with a center object and a second overlapping object, one central fixation/dot design, and COCO instance masks as the object ground truth. This may not capture cases where human object perception diverges from dataset annotations, parts, stuff regions, or amodal/object-level grouping.

Statistical reporting is relatively light. The paper would be stronger with confidence intervals or significance tests for model differences, the object-centricity/behavior correlation, noise ceiling estimates, and Gram-alignment improvements.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and underexplored question: whether modern self-supervised vision models exhibit object grouping behavior aligned with human perception in natural scenes. I would assess it primarily as a dataset/benchmark and empirical analysis contribution rather than an algorithms paper, which makes the behavioral data collection and evaluation protocol central to its value.

The behavioral experiment is carefully designed: 72 participants, eye tracking, counterbalanced same/different and close/far conditions, high accuracy, and analyses of accuracy, sensitivity, bias, and reaction-time reliability. Scaling the classical two-dot paradigm to natural COCO scenes is a meaningful contribution.

The model evaluation is clear and well motivated. Comparing DINO/DINOv2/DINOv3, MAE, supervised ViTs, supervised ConvNeXts, and distilled ConvNext models gives a useful empirical picture of how architecture and training objective relate to object-centric representations.

The object-centric AUC metric based on patch affinities and COCO object masks is simple, interpretable, and well connected to the paper's main hypothesis. The reported correlation between this metric and human RT prediction is compelling as an empirical observation.

The Gram-alignment experiment strengthens the paper beyond a purely correlational model comparison by attempting an intervention on supervised models, and the CLS-token distillation baseline is a useful control.
The manuscript is generally well written, with clear figures, a coherent narrative, and adequate supplementary details on the behavioral analyses and readout training.
weaknesses: The main causal claims are stronger than the evidence fully supports. The model comparisons are confounded by objective, data scale, architecture, model family, implementation details, and pretraining corpus. The paper acknowledges partial confounding, but still repeatedly frames the DINO objective and Gram structure as key mechanisms.

The RT prediction setup would benefit from stronger non-visual and low-level baselines. For example, baselines using dot distance, same/different label, object mask geometry, object size, boundary distance, category identity, coordinates, or simple image statistics are needed to establish how much of the model-human correlation comes from learned visual representations rather than task geometry or annotation-derived structure.

The absolute behavioral alignment is modest: the best raw Spearman correlation is about 0.35 with a noise ceiling of 0.42. The normalized value of 0.83 sounds strong, but the raw predictive power should be emphasized more, and confidence intervals across folds/seeds/images would help judge robustness.

The object-centric AUC metric and the grouping task both rely heavily on COCO object masks and central/peripheral object membership. This makes it plausible that the AUC metric partly captures the same annotation-defined structure used to generate the task, rather than independently explaining human perceptual grouping difficulty.

The correlation between object-centric AUC and behavioral alignment is computed over only nine models. The reported p-value is therefore fragile, and model-family dependence may inflate the apparent strength of the relationship. More models, layers, sizes, objectives, and independently trained variants would make the conclusion more convincing.

The Gram-alignment experiment is suggestive but not definitive. Matching DINOv3 Gram matrices may transfer many teacher-specific properties besides object-centric pairwise structure, and the CLS baseline alone does not rule out other forms of dense-feature distillation or teacher-student regularization as explanations.

The benchmark is limited to COCO-style annotated objects with one central dot placed on an object and selected valid dot configurations. It is unclear how well the conclusions generalize to stuff regions, amorphous objects, occlusion-heavy scenes, non-COCO categories, or cases where human object perception diverges from instance annotations.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed in the manuscript text: it says code and data are available, but the provided PDF text does not include an actual link, and important details such as hyperparameter search ranges, exact pretrained checkpoints, and Gram-alignment training schedule are limited.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting and ECCV-relevant question: whether modern self-supervised vision models organize natural scenes in a way that resembles human object grouping. The two-dot behavioral paradigm is well motivated by psychophysics, and scaling it to COCO scenes with eye tracking and counterbalancing gives the work a useful empirical basis.

The manuscript compares several model families and training regimes, including DINO/DINOv2/DINOv3, MAE, supervised ViTs, and ConvNeXt variants. The reported ordering is plausible and consistent across grouping accuracy, RT prediction, and the proposed object-centricity metric.
The object-centric ROC/AUC analysis of patch affinity maps is intuitive and helps connect model behavior to representational structure rather than reporting only black-box predictive accuracy.

The supplementary material includes some useful checks, including behavioral accuracy/sensitivity, a linear readout baseline, condition-split correlations, and a CLS-token distillation baseline for the Gram-alignment experiment.
weaknesses: The main behavioral-alignment evaluation appears vulnerable to data leakage: the 1,020 examples are the four dot-placement conditions for the same 255 images, but the nested cross-validation is described as trial-level rather than image-level. If different conditions from the same image can appear in both train and test folds, the readout may exploit image-specific content or difficulty. This is a serious concern because trial-by-trial RT prediction is one of the central claims.

The empirical evidence is weaker than the framing suggests. The best raw model-human Spearman correlation is only 0.348, with a noise ceiling of 0.42; the normalized score of 0.83 makes the result look much stronger. The paper should foreground the raw effect sizes and uncertainty, and should provide confidence intervals or statistical tests for model differences, not just rankings.

The paper claims that training objective is the key factor, but architecture, data scale, model generation, distillation, and pretraining corpus are not cleanly disentangled. For example, DINOv3 ConvNeXt is distilled from a transformer teacher, and DINOv3 differs from earlier models in more than objective. With only nine models, the very high cross-model correlation between object-centric AUC and behavioral alignment is suggestive but not robust evidence for a general principle.

The proposed object-centricity metric relies on COCO instance masks, the same annotation source used to construct stimuli and dot placements. It therefore measures agreement with dataset semantic masks more than human perceptual grouping, especially in ambiguous, occluded, part-whole, or stuff/object cases. This weakens the claim that the metric captures human-like grouping rather than segmentation-mask alignment.

The RT readout is supervised on the behavioral data, so strong performance does not by itself show that the backbone intrinsically predicts human grouping difficulty. The linear baseline helps, but the paper still needs stronger controls, such as image-held-out evaluation, simple geometric/semantic baselines, mask-distance baselines, and readouts using only COCO labels or object-mask features.

The Gram-alignment experiment is overinterpreted. Distilling the Gram matrix from DINOv3 predictably transfers DINOv3-like dense similarity structure, but this does not establish Gram structure as a mechanism underlying human-like perception. The experiment lacks sufficient controls over teacher choice, distillation target, fine-tuning compute, and held-out generalization, and the main paper reports mostly qualitative plot-based improvements rather than precise numbers and uncertainty.

The contribution type is closer to Datasets/Benchmarks or Applied/Systems than Algorithms/General. Under a benchmark-style assessment, the behavioral dataset and analysis are useful, but the benchmark is small by CV standards, depends on COCO masks, and lacks a clear public link despite the placeholder claim that code and data are available. Under Algorithms/General, the algorithmic novelty is limited.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript says code and data are available “here” but provides no actual link; the dot-placement algorithm, exact checkpoints, preprocessing, split construction, and Gram-alignment training schedule are not specified in enough detail to reproduce the central results confidently.

The writing is generally clear, but the claims are too strong relative to the evidence, especially statements that self-supervised transformers capture object structure in a behaviorally human-like manner and that Gram matrix structure drives perceptual alignment. The paper would be more convincing if framed as a promising correlational benchmark study rather than a mechanistic account.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and timely question: whether the object grouping structure emerging in self-supervised vision models aligns with human perceptual grouping in natural scenes. This is a meaningful contribution to computer vision because it connects dense representation quality, object-centric structure, and behavioral human alignment rather than only downstream benchmark accuracy.

The behavioral benchmark is well motivated and substantially richer than classical two-dot psychophysics studies: 72 participants, controlled same/different and close/far conditions, eye tracking, counterbalancing, high accuracy, and supplementary checks on sensitivity, bias, and reaction-time signal reliability. The experiment appears carefully designed.

The model comparison is broad enough to support the main empirical pattern: DINO-style self-supervised ViTs outperform supervised ViTs with the same base architecture, MAE is intermediate, and a DINOv3-distilled ConvNext improves over supervised ConvNexts. This triangulates the role of training objective while also showing architecture is not the only factor.

The proposed object-centricity metric based on patch affinity ROC/AUC is simple, interpretable, and well aligned with the paper's claims. The strong correlation between this metric and human RT prediction across models is one of the clearest pieces of evidence in the paper.

The Gram alignment experiment strengthens the paper beyond a passive model comparison. Fine-tuning supervised models to match the DINOv3 Gram structure improves grouping accuracy, object-centric AUC, and behavioral alignment, and the CLS-token distillation baseline helps isolate patch-level pairwise structure as the relevant ingredient.

The manuscript is clearly written, with good connections to perceptual grouping, object binding, self-supervised dense features, and recent DINO work. The supplementary material usefully reports raw correlations, condition-wise analyses, and implementation details.
weaknesses: The behavioral RT prediction evaluation may suffer from image-level leakage. The 1,020 trials come from 255 images under four dot conditions, but the described 10-fold cross-validation appears to split trials rather than images. If different conditions from the same image appear in both train and test folds, the readout may exploit image-specific structure, reducing confidence that the reported RT correlations reflect generalization to unseen scenes. An image-level split would be an important control.

The strongest normalized behavioral result is based on a raw Spearman correlation of 0.348 against a relatively low noise ceiling of 0.42. The normalized value of 0.83 is encouraging, but the absolute predictive relationship remains moderate. The paper should emphasize this more carefully and provide confidence intervals or statistical comparisons between models.

The claims about training objective versus architecture are plausible but still partly confounded by scale, data, pretraining recipe, and model family. The authors acknowledge this, but the conclusion sometimes reads more causally than the experimental design fully supports.

The Gram alignment results are promising but not yet a complete mechanistic demonstration. Since the teacher is DINOv3 ViT-B, improvements could reflect broad teacher distillation effects beyond Gram structure, despite the useful CLS baseline. Additional baselines such as feature-token distillation, random/low-rank Gram targets, or within-family teacher controls would make the causal interpretation stronger.

The object-centricity metric relies on COCO object annotations and patch-level within/outside-object labels, which may favor models whose representations align with COCO category/object definitions. It is less clear how well the conclusions transfer to non-COCO images, stuff regions, ambiguous object boundaries, occlusion-heavy scenes, or object parts where human grouping may diverge from dataset annotations.

The model set is useful but still limited. Important comparators such as CLIP/vision-language models, segmentation-specialized backbones, larger/smaller DINO variants, and more controlled architecture-scale matched models would help establish how general the findings are.

Reproducibility is reasonable in outline but incomplete in the manuscript text: exact checkpoints, preprocessing details, random seeds, code/data URL, and details of the Gram-alignment training dataset and schedule should be made fully explicit. The phrase 'Code and data are available here' appears without an actual accessible link in the manuscript text I reviewed.
